business.what_it_does: Plausible is a simple, privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics — a lightweight analytics script and one-page dashboard that measures website traffic without cookies or personal data collection.

facts.statement: Plausible does not use cookies and does not collect personal data; no IP addresses, device fingerprints or persistent identifiers are collected.

provenance.quote: No personal data is collected. No IP addresses, device fingerprints or persistent identifiers of any kind.

facts.statement: All visitor data is processed and stored in the EU on EU-owned servers; data never leaves the EU.

provenance.quote: All data is processed and stored in the EU on servers owned by European companies. Data never leaves the EU.

facts.statement: Google Analytics loads 135KB of JavaScript per new visitor; Plausible's script is 2.5KB and needs no cookie banner.

provenance.quote: Google Analytics loads 135KB of JavaScript for every new visitor. Plausible loads 2.5KB and needs no cookie banner on top.

facts.statement: Plausible has never spent money on advertising, affiliates or paid endorsements; it grows through word of mouth.

provenance.quote: We have never spent a cent on advertising, affiliates or paid endorsements. Plausible grows because people recommend it when they have no reason to other than that it works.

facts.statement: Plausible tracks visits from AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini, including which pages they land on and whether those visitors complete goals.

provenance.quote: Track and analyze real visits your website gets from AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Gemini, etc. See which pages attract clicks, how well they engage and whether those visitors complete business goals.

facts.statement: Customers of Plausible include Stripe, Mozilla, Basecamp, Ghost, Hugging Face, Home Assistant, MongoDB, the Python Software Foundation and Harvard University.

provenance.quote: An independent review by a data protection lawyer confirms Plausible requires no cookie consent and falls outside the scope of GDPR personal data processing.

segments.name: A developer-founder who publishes to a technical audience and no longer believes his own Google Analytics numbers
segments.situation: He owns the whole surface: a blog or newsletter sitting next to a product or docs site, a stack he chose himself, script tags he pastes by hand. His readers are the Hacker News and Reddit crowd, which Plausible's own comparisons describe as blocking Google Analytics at rates around 40–58%, so the dashboard he checks after a launch is very likely reporting a fraction of what happened. GA4 answers go three menus deep or require building an Exploration from scratch, and the one question he actually has — which post sent people who signed up — is the one that takes longest to get. He also carries a cookie banner on an otherwise fast, hand-built page, and the only thing that put it there is the analytics tag. He is likely already running peers' recommendations: people in his circle name Plausible out loud, and the company has never paid for that.

segments.name: The person inside a privacy-constrained institution who has to get an analytics tool past legal, security and procurement
segments.situation: She works somewhere — a university, a public body, an open-source company — where anything that touches visitor data goes through a vendor review before it goes live. Google Analytics is not a neutral default in her building: European data protection authorities have been found to rule against it on EU–US transfers, and that argument has a habit of reopening at renewal. Her review pack needs a DPA she does not have to chase, a clear answer on where data is stored, a security page she can forward, and SSO for her identity provider. Plausible's own position is that it is straightforward to approve because the product collects no personal data, sets no cookies and keeps data in the EU, and it names Hugging Face, Harvard and the Scottish and Welsh governments as organisations that completed that review. Whether the dashboard is pretty matters far less to her than whether it survives the questionnaire without a quarter of back-and-forth.

situation_provenance.quote: Plausible is typically straightforward to approve in vendor reviews. Not because of optimized paperwork, but because the product does not collect personal data, does not use cookies and does not send data outside the EU.
Organizations like Hugging Face, Harvard and the Scottish and Welsh governments have completed this review and run Plausible at scale.
Is Google Analytics illegal? Multiple European Data Protection Authorities have found it to be in violation of GDPR due to EU-US data transfers.

objections.objection: Google Analytics is free. I would be creating a recurring line item for something I currently get for nothing — and even the people recommending Plausible say outright that it is not free.
objections.answer: The evidence publishes no price for any plan, so the copy cannot argue value for money with a number and must not invent one. What it can do is remove the cost of deciding: a 30-day free trial with no credit card and no automatic charges, two months free on annual billing, discounted nonprofit and education plans, and an explicit suggestion to run Plausible alongside Google Analytics during the trial and compare the traffic numbers before paying anything.

provenance.quote: My 100% favorite GA4 alternative so far is Plausible. Not free and not a ton of bells and whistles, but SOOOO easy to use (for clients too) and the data is near real-time. A good solution for ~70% of websites struggling with GA4.

objections.objection: A single one-page dashboard cannot answer the questions I take to GA4. I will lose custom reports, multi-dimension tables and anything I need to assemble for a client or a board.
objections.answer: The official Data Studio connector is built and maintained by Plausible and reads the same data as the dashboard through the Stats API: multi-dimension tables, stacked charts, conditional formatting, running totals and calculated fields, blended with Google Ads spend, Meta campaign data or a revenue-target Google Sheet, exported as branded PDFs or shared as a live link, with several sites in one report. The honest limit is that it sits on the Business plan. Inside the product itself: funnels, user journeys, saved segments, custom properties, scroll depth and the Stats API.

provenance.quote: The standard objection to privacy-first analytics is “but it doesn’t let me build custom reports.”

objections.objection: Switching costs me years of history and a weekend of rebuilding goals and tags that currently work.
objections.answer: The Google Analytics importer brings historical data across, and both Universal Analytics and GA4 properties can be imported into the same dashboard with time ranges detected automatically to avoid double counting or gaps; GA4 imports now include custom events. Installation is a WordPress plugin or a code-free Google Tag Manager template, enhanced measurements are picked from a checklist that generates the snippet, and a testing tool sends test traffic and tells you what is wrong. It can run alongside Google Analytics during the trial. Two limits the evidence itself states: imported stats stop at your first Plausible visitor, and filtering of imported data is limited compared with native data.

objections.objection: Nothing is actually broken. We already have GA4, or our platform reports traffic for us, so this is a solution to a problem I have not felt.
objections.answer: The claim to attack is that the existing numbers are wrong, not that the interface is unpleasant. Consent declines are said — via a linked independent study — to leave more than half the data missing; 58% of tech audiences and 40%+ of a tech site's audience are reported to block Google Analytics; Brave and uBlock Origin block it by default; Google Analytics sets cookies, which is what forces the banner; in Plausible's own simulated-bot test GA4 counted the bots as real users while Plausible excluded them; and every visitor downloads 135KB less JavaScript. Note for the writer: apart from the linked study, these are Plausible's own comparisons about a rival, not independent verification.

objections.objection: Legal will not accept a vendor's own website telling us we do not need consent. That is exactly the kind of assurance we are supposed to challenge.
objections.answer: The strongest answer in the evidence is not a vendor sentence: an independent review by a data protection lawyer concludes Plausible requires no cookie consent and falls outside the scope of GDPR personal data processing, and the full assessment is published. Around it: a DPA in place automatically for every customer, covering processor responsibilities, data location, a 48-hour breach notification obligation and subprocessor controls; all processing and storage in the EU on EU-owned servers (Hetzner, Germany) with data never leaving the EU; raw IP address and User-Agent never written to logs, databases or disk and the hashing salt rotated and deleted every 24 hours; source code publicly available for independent audit. And a precedent list: Hugging Face, Harvard and the Scottish and Welsh governments have completed this review.

provenance.quote: An independent review by a data protection lawyer confirms Plausible requires no cookie consent and falls outside the scope of GDPR personal data processing.

objections.objection: Procurement requires a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report and a contractual uptime SLA. Self-published security pages do not clear our bar.
objections.answer: This cannot be beaten with what we currently know, and the copy must not imply otherwise. Nothing in the evidence names a security certification, an external auditor or a compliance attestation — the compliance material is self-published documentation plus a lawyer's privacy review, and the security page explicitly states that Plausible aims to provide continuous availability but does not guarantee uninterrupted service. What can be forwarded, as documented practice rather than certification: daily encrypted backups retained 30 days in the EU with restore tests at least quarterly, round-the-clock monitoring with on-call paging, a public status page with current and historical uptime, a formal incident response plan with drills and post-incident reviews, business continuity and disaster recovery plans reviewed annually, peer review where authors cannot approve their own changes, a vulnerability disclosure programme, and a single compliance page built for vendor reviews.

objections.objection: Ad blockers will block Plausible too. I would be trading one set of missing visitors for another and paying for the privilege.
objections.answer: Partially answerable. Plausible's own position is that it can be blocked but far less often than privacy-invasive tools such as Google Analytics — unquantified, and their claim about themselves. The concrete fix in the evidence is the proxy: run the script as a first-party connection from your own domain to bypass most remaining blocks and get more accurate, often higher, counts. The caveat worth naming rather than hiding: the managed proxy is Enterprise-only, so on lower plans you set the proxy up yourself, and no independent measurement of Plausible's own block rate exists in the evidence.

objections.objection: I run more sites and more people than the published plans allow, and there is no price for my size — so I cannot work out what this costs me before I start a conversation.
objections.answer: Partially answerable. The tiers are explicit on limits: Growth is up to 3 sites and 3 team members; Business is up to 10 sites, 10 team members, 5 years of retention, Stats API at 600 requests per hour, ecommerce revenue attribution and the Data Studio connector; Enterprise covers 600+ API requests per hour, SSO, managed proxy, scheduled raw event exports, 5+ years of retention and priority support. Agencies and freelancers are a named use case with multi-site management and client reporting, and one connector report can pull several sites. What the evidence does not give is any price, or any site allowance above 10 — so the copy can describe the ceiling honestly and point to contact, but must not quote a number.

objections.objection: It is open source and the Community Edition is free to self-host. Why would I pay a subscription for software I can run myself?
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence argues against self-hosting, and pretending otherwise would be dishonest: the Community Edition is described by Plausible as "free as in beer", self-hosted and AGPL-licensed, and the forkability is sold as a feature — customers are not locked in and the code can be forked if Plausible ever acted against its stated values. What the paid service documents is the operating work you would otherwise own: encrypted storage in Germany on Hetzner servers, daily automated backups with AES-256 encryption and at-least-quarterly restore tests, round-the-clock monitoring with on-call paging, DDoS shielding at the CDN, updates deployed multiple times a week with peer review, automated testing and a rollback plan for every change, and a DPA in place automatically.

provenance.quote: There’s always been a [strong interest](https://github.com/plausible/analytics/issues/26) from the community to self-host the code.

objections.objection: My clients and stakeholders ask for Google Analytics by name. Explaining why their reports now come from something they have never heard of is a conversation I do not want.
objections.answer: Only partially answerable. Nothing in the evidence addresses a client who insists on the Google Analytics brand. What it does support: a working consultant's public account that Plausible is easy to use for clients too; branded Data Studio dashboards with your own logo and only the metrics that client cares about, exported as PDF or shared as a live link; private shared links that remember the password so the client does not retype it, and that can be limited to a single filtered segment; weekly or monthly email reports that reach stakeholders without a login.
